title: Three tools, one repo
spec: M05 · same fifteen files, three artifacts
intro: Point Graphify, CodeGraph and okf-rs at the same monorepo. They disagree about what a node is, where the graph should live, and how it stays fresh — and all three are right. The output is a decision table, not a ranking.

provenance.source: a replayed comparison over labs/sample-project. The node, edge and provenance counts are reproducible with labs/shared_tools/kg_extract.py; the seven-project table in step 4 is CodeGraph's own vendor-published benchmark, labelled as such in the narrative; step 5 carries its own measured citation.

foot: Build the matrix for your own repo with M05's four-step exercise — no lab folder, it runs on your real project.

steps.title: Three commands, three artifacts
narrative: orderflow is fifteen files: a billing service, an orders service, a notifications worker, three shared modules, three docs. Small enough that you can check every answer by hand — which is the only way to compare tools honestly.

Run all three over it. Watch the counts on the right, because the first surprise arrives before you have asked a single question: the three tools do not agree on how many things are in this repo. That is not one of them being wrong. It is three different answers to "what is a node?"
steps.youDo: cd labs/sample-project, then run the three builds in turn. Nothing here asks for an API key — every one of these passes is deterministic.

steps.title: Ask the same question three ways
narrative: Now the query surface — axis 5, and the axis you feel every day. Ask the question an agent asks constantly: who calls decode_jwt?

Three tools, three routes to the same true answer. CodeGraph answers in one MCP tool call with snippets attached. okf-rs answers by being a file you can read — cat the concept and the CalledBy list is already written down, no runtime involved. Graphify answers through its CLI or skill and hands back a structured object with a blast radius on it.

The differences are not cosmetic. One is a database you must query, one is text you can grep and diff in a pull request, one is an artifact set with a human-readable report. Pick by how your team actually works, not by which log line is prettiest.
steps.youDo: Register the okf-rs server once — claude mcp add okf-rs -- /path/to/okf-mcp /path/to/project — then ask the same question through each surface and check all three against the ground-truth list at the bottom of labs/sample-project/README.md.
steps.claudeSays: Whichever surface answers, the assistant reasons over the returned relationships. shared/auth.py never enters the context window.

view.text: If your team reviews knowledge the way it reviews code — in pull requests, line by line — okf-rs's substrate wins before any benchmark is opened, because a database diff is unreadable and a Markdown diff is a review comment. If your team wants an agent to get one answer with zero ceremony, CodeGraph's single-call surface wins. Neither of those is a performance argument.

steps.title: What each one will not tell you
narrative: Every tool has a shape of question it answers confidently and wrongly. These are the failure modes, and they are the part no launch post contains.

Watch the terminal. okf-rs validate passing is a real signal — the bundle is well-formed, no dangling links, no Calls/CalledBy asymmetry. It is not a signal that the bundle is true. Those are different questions, and only the second one matters to an agent about to refactor your payments code.
steps.youDo: Run the CI recipe the module gives you — okf-rs generate --no-cache && okf-rs validate --ci — on a bundle you have not regenerated since your last commit. --ci hardens warnings into failures, which is the only setting worth running.

terminal.text: "no issues found" answers is it well-formed? — not is it still true?
error: 4 concepts differ from a fresh generate — bundle is stale

state.label: the blind spot in each design

cells: on orderflow, 13 of the 22 edges are name-resolution guesses and 9 are read off the syntax tree. CodeGraph hands you all 22 with the same confidence
deterministic, and exactly as current as your last generate
--enrich writes LLM prose into missing descriptions. It never overwrites an existing one, but it also never tells the reader which sentences a model wrote
sync is hooks or manual — no watchers, no stale flag
the graph drifts from the code and nothing announces it. M11 is an entire postmortem on this
returns similarity-ranked leads the agent must verify by opening files, where a structural graph returns answers
the one design that handles its own failure
unsynced files are explicitly flagged stale, telling agents to read them directly. This is the layer everyone else is missing

steps.title: The best benchmark in the field, and the shape hiding in it
narrative: CodeGraph's team published the most careful comparison anyone has run: seven real open-source projects in seven languages, identical exploration tasks, the same model in headless mode (claude -p), four runs per arm, medians reported, the sole variable being whether the graph was available. It is vendor-reported — read it as such — but the methodology is serious.

Aggregates: 57% fewer tokens, 71% fewer tool calls, 46% faster, 35% cheaper. Now stop reading the aggregate and read the spread. The per-project column runs from 13% to 90%, and the ordering is not random.

Savings track repo size. Rust benefits most, because mod / use / pub use re-exports punish agent traversal hardest. And small repos see almost nothing — the ~500-file floor again, now with per-language evidence. Same model in both arms, so none of this is the model getting smarter; every saved token was mechanical exploration deleted.

state.label: CodeGraph's 7-project benchmark · vendor-reported, medians of 4 runs

view.text: 1 — size correlates with savings. The larger the haystack, the more an agent flails without a map. 2 — Rust benefits disproportionately, because its module system creates the exploration paths that cost most to walk. 3 — small repos see diminishing returns: 13% on OkHttp, 34% on Gin. Pair every one of those rows with the aggregate before you quote it, and notice that a 57% headline is doing a lot of work to hide a 13%.

steps.title: The decision table — choosing, not ranking
narrative: There is no winner row here, and any table that produces one is selling something. What there is, is a set of constraints you already have, each of which eliminates candidates before benchmarks are relevant.

Run your own requirement down the left column. Most teams find that two axes decide the whole thing and the other four are tie-breakers — and which two decide is a property of your organisation, not of the tools.
Then toggle to the pane that keeps you honest: on a repo below the floor, the correct answer is none of them, and the measured evidence for that is unkind to everything on this page.
steps.youDo: Fill the six axes for your own repo: count files with git ls-files | wc -l, write the requirement your environment imposes on each axis, then install only the tool the matrix points to and verify three answers by hand.

after.title: MEASURED — the floor, on a real 36-file repo

view.text: Capstone 2 ran a four-arm campaign on a 36-file Spring Boot service: four questions, three fresh sessions per cell, 48 sessions. Every graph configuration lost. The cheapest arm was a single 55-line root CLAUDE.md; the most expensive was the graph forced on with file access removed. That is the same finding CodeGraph's OkHttp row shows at 13%, arrived at independently and from the other direction. The six axes tell you which tool. The file count tells you whether to install one at all.
